sentences.text: Hello, Andy.
This meeting is being recorded.
Hi, Robin, how you doing?
I'm doing well.
How about yourself?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
I'm good.
Are we related?
I'm wondering.
We're related at some point in time.
Right, yeah, of course, we all were.
Whereabouts is your family from anywhere in particular?
Well, incidentally, my middle name is Andrew so that's, that's, that's making it very, very close.
But so my grandparents on my father's side would be immigrants from England.
So this is between the wars coming over.
I meet a lot of days I meet, meet some Robins.
It's rare that I meet someone who has two of my names.
So that's a, that's a funny coincidence.
Do you know where in the UK they came from?
Pardon me?
Do you know what?
I'm not sure because I feel like it's Sussex, but I, I don't know.
Okay.
Yeah, it could be my, my family's from Bedfordshire and they go back quite a few generations but I tend to meet quite a lot of days from that area which is the south east.
So Sussexes.
So maybe a relations somewhere.
All right, well, I know Maggie's trying to get off another call that she's on so she should be joining shortly.
Yeah, she wasn't there so I was giving you a few minutes for her to join but she, she hasn't joined by four or five minutes in, so I thought we better get started.
Sure.
So.
So basically, you know, obviously we reached out to you.
I, I initially had gotten an email from you through a blast about a year ago and I sort of put it on the side to keep it, keep it handy for when I needed it.
Just very quickly, you know, Maggie and I started this business, family business, over 30 years ago.
It's a pharmaceutical health related business.
We function.

The best way to describe it is to an outsider is that we function like a creative agency but we have a network of displays, print and digital in waiting areas of pharmacies and clinics across the country.
So essentially we develop content marketing.
Content if you, if you can think of health as being something that's marketed for those areas on behalf of sponsors which are primarily pharma.
So we are niche in that sense.
I think you guys kind of work with all different, different types of agencies.
Yeah, we do actually Robin.
So that's.
Yeah, I mean that's massively interesting.
So I'm definitely keen to get into that and find out a little bit more in terms of the pharma side of things.
Yeah, we've Worked with agencies that work in the pharma space.
Some of the, well, they're all pretty big, aren't they?
But some of the really big ones in the US and also, funnily enough.
We work.
On the network and display stuff as well, but completely different business in retail, in the supermarket space, Shopper media.
Okay, so very familiar with both of those aspects, but never, never at the same time.
So, I mean, I should say that, you know, we're our main, you know, we're not young, we're not spring chickens anymore.
And if we were, we probably wouldn't be having this conversation because, you know, our primary focus, even at our age is growth.
We still want to grow the business.
We're looking for the right, the right partner, the right combination of companies to help us grow that business.
We have to have a, an exit strategy just because of our age.
You know, I think it's just.
I'm 70 actually.
Maggie's 69.
You know, we're not, we're not young, so we need to do this or get ourselves in a position where if our health touch wood doesn't hold out, that we're not caught, you know, in a bad position.
So we've got to be, it's a, it's part of a planning process.
It's not that we want to stop working.
We actually are quite energized by, by the challenge and by things that are going on and just by the growth of the growth, growth of the company and the growth prospects.
So just to let you know, that's kind of where we're at with that.
And we have done quite a bit of work, prep work, so we've prepared a very comprehensive SIM already.
So this saves a lot of work, a lot of back and forth between us.
And you will be the first one to have seen the sim.
We really felt it was necessary because of the niche nature of the business.

It will help someone understand who we are, what's the environment that we're in, what we, where we think the growth is, what kind of combinations would work well with us and other people if we were put together?
Market valuation, financials, the whole, the whole thing.
Happy to share that with you.
If we just get an NDA out of the way and get that over to you so you can look at it.
Yeah, that, that sounds interesting.
Definitely.
All right, so it's good to get the, the kind of overview of where you're at.
I don't know how much you know about us.
Obviously you've done a Google search for sell Your marketing agency or something similar and we would have come, come up top, top four that.
But we are, we're capital A, we're an M and A advisory and we work exclusively in the marketing agency space.
So all of our clients are either buyers or sellers of marketing agencies.
Sometimes the buyers are private equity but usually they're sort of high growth agencies that are looking to acquire through inorganic growth.

So yeah, we're very, very sort of niched it in this space and like I say, although we haven't come across a pharma sort of, you know, display network or market advertising network, whatever you are calling it out of home do you call it?
But we've definitely come up with slightly different combinations before with clients so I think we could definitely help you.
We work on the sell side as Agencies Co.
So we have a platform that we own which is Agencies Co, which is a marketplace for buyers and sellers and marketing agencies and on that platform we have about 20,000 newsletter subscribers.
But also as a business we have 130,000 agencies and buyers of agencies in our CRM as well.
So we've got really, really strong reach from that point of view.
And yeah, I guess in terms of where you are Robin, what would you say is the sort of next steps that you're looking to do?
Because obviously if you've prepared a SIM already, you've obviously put a lot of thought into whether it's the right time to go to the market or not.
But, but is it, is it imminent or are you looking to sort of, you know, find out more about what an M and A would look like or.

No, no, I mean we're quite, we've done quite a bit of work on this and we have a very good idea of what we're getting into and we've had evaluation done, we've just, we've just done a lot of prep work to really get a handle on, on as, as much of this as we can.
This isn't what we do every day.
So it, it, it takes us, it would take us probably much longer than it would for you to put together the same content.
But we did do it, spent a lot of time on it last over the past 12 months.
It is done.
So you know, I think that as I mentioned before, we've had good growth.
We've got, there's a very high profit margin.
Small.
We're a small company, we're not huge small but we're growing very nicely and we have some very good growth prospects just organically as well as if you Start to look at some combinations.
So next steps for me, I'd like to share this information with you.

And then if you want, we could, you know, there are some, there are some buy potential buyers who are already in our space in the US Primarily in Canada, we're kind of it, you know, we're the most important company in Canada.
But in the US you've got big players and you have to get there.
They're an obvious group that you've got to go to and say, do you want to do this?
In Canada our regulations are different than theirs and they're closer to yours, actually.
But we make a case for what we think the market's worth here, you know, to a, to somebody who's from down there and try to give them as much of a feel in the sim of what that could look like.
So we've got that.

Then the other piece is to look at some of these other combinations even of just Canadian companies, to say if you put these companies together, then you've really got this, you're really taking this point of care marketing channel, as we call it, which is developing and you really kind of establish it as a must do tactic.
This is what we're trying to do strategically.
So you know, you have television, you have social media, you have, you have these main channels that are available to marketers and in the pharma space they talk.
The buzzword is omnichannel.
And this really means targeting patients and with the right, with the information at different parts of the journey.
So for us, we're doing it when they're just about to see the health professional.
And that's when the treatment decision's made, that's when the choice of drug is made.

So if you're influencing them conversationally, not talking about telling them about a brand here, but if you're influencing them conversationally, that's the role of the point of care marketing piece in that omnichannel strategy.
And it's the only one that does it in that place at that critical moment.
So that's the advantage that it really has.
And if we can develop this.
I think Maggie just joined actually.
Hello, Andy.
Sorry, I was stuck at another meeting.
No problem.
No problem at all.
Okay, cool.
All right, so well, let's just start at the beginning of that then, Robin.
So in terms of your sim that you've got, it sounds like you filled it with information that possibly wouldn't have the background to put in there.
But what are the basics, you know, what's your revenue today?
You know either last full financial year or trailing 12 months, however you work it.
And what is the margin on the business at the moment?
The, the billings are three and a half million.
Forecasted.
Yeah.
Forecasted to go to 4 this year.
Budgeted to go to 4 this year.
Profit margin is in excess of EBITDA, if you want to put it that way, is in excess of 40%.
Wow, that's massive.

And it has been this high consistently and it took a long time to establish this network and it was years actually to put together all of these displays in the various places that we have and to develop these relations with people who have these TV screens that we use.
But all of that is sort of money spent.
And right now we have operationally where we've developed a very good infrastructure using Salesforce for deployment and management of all of our materials that goes out.
And this allows us to be very, very profitable.
And this is, this is fully scalable.
What's interesting to know is we don't pay the pharmacies and the clinics to post our information in their waiting room.
We position it as a value added service.
Turnkey changed every three months.
We have four E reps on the road that go in, change the poster, give material to the doctor.
Okay.
So it's printed.
Printed.
And we have both.
Yeah, we have both as well.
Okay.
In terms of the printing, we, in this case, so we do all the content development.
So we've, we've, we work with the clients and develop a strategy for them for messaging.
And the messaging has to fit their needs, it has to fit the patient's needs, has to resonate with them, and it has to fit the healthcare professional's needs as well.
They want quality information in their waiting areas that's helping them as well as their patients.
So we have to fulfill this broadcast range of needs.
So we, we have the expertise for this.
So we develop it, design it, print it for all the sites that we have metal frames on the walls of these waiting rooms.
They're all out there.
So we go in and our people, I can refer to them as reps, our installers go into these locations and physically change those materials.
And this is a little more than.
You saw a picture, Robin?
No, I, I haven't, we haven't quite got that far yet, but.
Okay.
But then digitally we work with, there's other companies and they have, they manage TV screens and waiting rooms for a collection of clinics, let's say, or pharmacies.
And we supply them with digital poster assets.
So this is basically a video record runtime, usually 45 seconds to a minute.
And it's the same principles or terms of content are applied to those and they deploy them on our behalf.
So we manage again, all of that through our infrastructure.
Okay, so you're looking at two options by the sounds of it.
So you're looking at an exit and what that would, would look like.
And you're also thinking about maybe some kind of rollup strategy with some other similar businesses, I'm guessing in Canada.
So can, can you give me a little bit more around your thoughts around the valuation and what you're looking to achieve, you know, in order for you guys to, to sell them?
Well, you know, it's.
Valuation has to be.
We're just looking to get a fair price.
You know, normally, I know in the agency business, the, I think the EBITDAs for a company our size are in the five.
The EBITDA multiples are in the five range.
You know, you, you could probably argue that there's.
Ours should be a bit higher than that because we have all these, this network of assets that are out there that have, have this life that will continue long after clients come and go.
And it's just, it's an asset that's out there that has, that has value.
But we can talk about, you know, what that's worth.
So, you know, I think we just want to make sure we get fair value for it.
We're, we're not.
That's all we want.
You know, we'd like to have the right buyer.
We, we want, we think we would like to be working with these people for a couple of years.
You know, we want to be, we see ourselves being there in a transition.
We want to have people that can, we want to have the right people to be part of that.
And we'd like to, you know, if there's growth that we're going to have together, we'd like to be rewarded for that additional growth as well.
We just don't want too much, but we just want to, we know we want as much as favorable as an environment as we can get in terms of, you know, the right profile of buyer.
Yeah.
So of the business that you do.

So it sounds like you, you've got sort of various services or I guess the way that you structure your fees is based on how much design work you're doing, how much advertising the client would buy with you, and then you've got your actual network fees or whatever else on top of it for delivery.
It's much simpler than that.
We basically sell space and we stay away from quantifying development time spent and all of this.
And we do this to get away from procurement pressure on, on, you know, so they, well, they say, well we normally only pay this much per hour for this type of service.
So we want you down to this range.
This way we control our pricing and we can say, look, you're buying space is how we put it to them within an environment.
We'll develop the content for that environment because that's our expertise.
But you're buying the space.
And this way we don't even have to manage all of these hours.
So some, some projects are very simple to execute, some are much more complicated.
We don't administer, you know, we keep track, let's say of our costs internally, but we don't keep track of hours.
We're just spending money keeping track of things when we could just be keeping that as profit.
So over the years it's just a much simpler model for us to work with.
What does a typical client spend with you then?
What would sort of an average client look like?
I'm going to let Maggie answer that.
I'm just going to get my door here.
It will be an average of a six month program either in the clinics or in the pharmacy, the print one and that will be 120,000 four is six months campaign.
If they come in a six month campaign, we would develop two different posters and we also offer them a one year campaign which will be like 10% less expensive.
And it's the same idea for digital.
It's a six month campaign minimum with two animations or one year campaign with four animations.
And the prices are pretty similar between poster and digital.
Okay, and then how many clients would you say that you normally have on a month to month basis?
Okay, we publish on a quarterly basis.
We can accommodate between all our.
Let's take printed.
I'll separate printed from digital because digital is bigger.
So every quarter for printed we can have around eight different sponsors between the pharmacies and the clinic.
For the digital we could have up to 20 different sponsors.
But we don't go all the way to 20.
Okay.
Sorry, big thing.
I was just going to.
Sorry Andy.
The big thing with us is that we have repeat, very high repeat business.
Situation, very repeat business in a period over two years.
So the, so it's a smaller clientele group obviously pharma primarily.
I mean we have some non pharma clients.
Therefore you have to be able to year over year be attractive to the same people.
But we've had people run campaigns for full years.
We've had people run them for two years straight, no interruption.
We've even had some run it for three years straight, no interruption.
Some of them run it continuously for three years, some of them sort of in three years over different periods, people repeating campaigns for seven years.
So we have a nice, we have a very solid reputation, a very good reputation for success for our clients and deliverables.
And the only thing holding us back from growing is the size of the network, which is expanding every year trying to get in more into specialty areas so we can.
The pharma industry is moving more into specialties.
We just want to make sure we can start to tap into some of those dollars that we haven't really done so far.
So that's the organic growth piece is if we, let's say we forget about everybody else and just look at ourselves just by being able to tap into specialty products.
So dermatology, neurology, things like this.
And these are revenues that are out there that we haven't even tapped into.
If we can expand our network into these type of special specialist offices, which is not easy to do, it's, it's takes.
Will take time to do it and we'll get a lot of very nice organic growth just from that.

And that's what our forecasts kind of, you look at this, you look at the sim, you see the forecast, you'll see the assumptions in there that we're going to be adding few of these specialties over time.
Actually, we are launching two specialty programs in 2026.
One, we have a partnership with Migraine Canada, so that's a plus.
And we will launch a program in migraine clinics across the country and we have a partnership with a dermatology patient association and we'll be launching also a program in that area.
So we're already starting going into specialty.
But we always have to have a partnership with the patient association and doctor association to sell it to the clinics and to the sponsors.
So what's the business model with the actual clinics themselves?
How are you able to avoid having to pay out to be in their space?
They just see it purely as informational products that they're getting for free.
Yeah, yeah.
The value has to be there.
We position it as a value added program.
So Mr.
Doctor, we're bringing you this information.
We come and change the posters for you every three months.
You don't have to do anything.
And that's why the doctors and the pharmacies like it.
You know, we, at some point, Andy, we could Take you through a case example of, you know, what the content was in the poster and how it benefits the three audiences.
So you could help visualize it a bit better.
Could save that up for another time if you want.
But if you're in the pharma world, you understand it intuitively right away.
But for someone who's not directly in that, you might need to see a couple of cases to show to understand it a bit better.
Yeah.
Okay, cool.
And, and so you've spent the time building the sim, have you, have you started marketing it yourself or whereabouts are you in the, the process of sort of launching?
We're, we're, we're starting with you.
Okay.
You know, we don't marketing it ourselves.
It's very time consuming for us.
It seems a little funny.
We, we could actually go out and approach some people and then we say there's other people.
It's a little bit awkward, especially if they're in Canada.
It's harder to do.
We just think we're, we want to, we just think we're better off probably having someone work on our behalf.
Okay.
Yeah, no, I think that's, that's, it's right.
It's, I think it's better, easier to have like the cushion of somebody else dealing with everybody and making those approaches.
Okay.
And then in terms of the, you said about the combinations, has that conversation ever progressed?
Did you ever approach anybody else about.
No.
And I think it just, you know, at this, we just don't have enough feel for how all that works.
I think we'd feel that we're going out there and we're just having some kind of experiment going on, talking to people and not quite sure how to orchestrate it.
It sounds like a complex thing to orchestrate.
Like I've got a vision of how it works.
So I'm going to go out and approach two different companies and say, you know what, we should get together because we could do this and that together.
And you have to be at a very, very senior level, first of all.
And they have to really know what you're up to.
And it can, we don't know if this could actually create some issues for us.
Yeah.
Because we just, we don't know what we don't know.
We have no experience with it, so we're a little bit uncomfortable doing it.
Okay, cool.
Yeah.
And our first choice really would be to find someone to sell the company to.
Okay.
Yes.
And then the second choice, if we can get a couple of companies together.
But that's a lot of Work and headaches, but it's a possibility.
Okay, and do you have timeline at all?
I know you said that you're happy to stay in for a couple of years, but is there a timeline that you're looking to, to get to market and then to stay in the business?
I mean we should, we're ready to, we're ready to go to market.
So for us, you know, all that's going to happen is we're going to keep growing, we're going to be worth a little more every year, we're going to get a little older.
That's about, that's about it.
That's all that's going to change.

We've done the work so I think we're ready to get started, you know, and we understand that first of all, we understand that someone will want to retain us, we think and secondly, we actually want to be retained because work is fun for us.
Yes, you're not looking to get out.
So, so just in the, in a normal run of the mill process usually the buyer like, likes the founders to stay in sometimes indefinitely but usually at least for three years.
That's kind of like the agency industry standard, but there are a million variations on that.
Something get out straight away or after a year and it all kind of affects the price in one way or another.
But founders that want to stay in, you tend to get that much more solid price.
The 5X is exactly right.
That is for the size of your business.
That's typical multiple for a marketing agency.
However, I don't know without looking into the financials and really how it works and understand it a bit better, I would say a marketing network is possibly worth more than that.
But again we'd have to get into it particularly around the digital side.

I would say even though the print side sounds like it is as successful, it is seen as a, you know, those sort of linear marketing channels are seen as businesses that are slowly sunsetting while the digital side of things is the growth area.
So but I would say possibly the 5x is possibly a little bit cheap.
So I think there might be more value in the business than that.
So let me take you through what we do.
So as I said before, we are, we have a marketing platform OurSagencies Co and really there's two sort of approaches that would suit what you're doing.

We've either got the gold or platinum and the difference between them is one is a very sort of structured six month process and really it suits sellers that are keen to get out of the business within A certain amount of time.
So we have a fairly sort of strict process that usually lasts around six months, sometimes a little bit longer, sometimes a little bit shorter.

And what we're doing is we're not only marketing on our platform and building all of the marketing materials that go with that, but also we're running a very structured process where we're looking to build up momentum within that campaign so that we have three or four buyers at the table.
And once we get one offer, we're able to then put a deadline on the deal and then sort of elicit those extra offers.
So we have for our client usually three or four different buyers with Lois that we can pick from and then we move forward with that.
And then it's usually about 30 days of due diligence and then around another 15 to 30 days of the contract.
So it usually is a 30 to 90 day process, which kind of brings us out the sort of six month mark.
Actually for smaller businesses, I would expect that sort of due diligence period to be a little bit shorter, around 30 days to 45 days really.
So that's like a daily process.
We meet with our clients on a weekly basis and we're looking to, to move that deal down the road, you know, on a daily basis.
One of my team will work on it daily.
So I don't know whether that would suit you guys because it sounds like you don't have that urgency really to get this deal done.
And it's not that we can't get a deal done as quick.
We actually have a very small package for small businesses and we've sold companies really quickly, you know, sort of three or four months to get it from start to finish to get a deal done.
But I think what would be more suitable for you guys is the gold package.
So for that what we're doing is we're creating all the marketing materials.
I know you've got SIM already, but we would still create the listing and the teaser and everything else that goes with that.
But also what we're building is a bespoke list of buyers.
So we have 20,000 agencies and agency buyers signed up to our mailing list and As I said, 130,000 in the CRM that we can do sort of keyword searches to look for matches.
But also we would build a very specific list for you of potential buyers as well.
So we would market to those.
Usually we get a good amount of feedback within the first 24 hours of going to market.
So we can usually tell if something is going to go or not.
But we are building a bespoke list and we are working our way through that list as well, trying to find the exact right buyer for you.
And usually we will get within sort of the first four or five weeks we will get buyers to the table that are interested in meeting with you.
And it, like I say, it usually takes about two or three months maximum to get that first offer and then we can sort of leverage that.
So I think the gold package is a bit more suitable.
But the main difference really is that we're not working on that on a daily basis and running a rigorous six month process, but we are following the process.
It's very similar in that we're sending out to our mailing list, it's listed on the agency's platform.
We're building that bespoke list of potential buyers that we're working our way through as well.
So I think of the two choices that's probably the most suitable from what I've said and what you guys have said as well.
The sort of six month rigorous process, not really what you're looking for.
Well, we don't, you know, we're not, we're not in a rush to do it to sell where we want to find the right buyer.
So we don't want to take forever doing it either.
But we just want to be efficient about it.

We definitely want to find the right people, we're going to live with them for two or three years, want to make sure that we can not just put up with each other, but we can actually grow, actually have some fun, you know, growing the business.
So.
Based off on what you've heard so far, you didn't get all the information.
What level of interest do you see in a company like ours?
Yeah, I think that there's going to be a lot of interest actually, Maggie.
I think there's two sort of levels of layers of interest, if you like.
I think you've got, you've got lots of marketing networks out there that own their own out of home or digital out of home networks.
I think instantly they, they would definitely be interested in the idea of being able to market into clinics very much.
I believe the out of home and digital out of home is going in that direction anyway, where we're not just advertising out in public spaces, you know, on bus stops or on the side of buildings.

I think, and I was just saying to Robin before, we actually have a client that has a shopper media marketing platform where they're able to actually even book marketing spaces on the edge of shelves and do all sorts of stuff like that.
It's very clever, actually.
So I think marketers are much more savvy and they're looking to go directly into different spaces.
So I think that the idea that you, you're building that client network, the clinic network, is very interesting.
So there would be those as buyers and then we also have a lot of agencies working in the pharma space with major pharmacy, pharmaceutical clients.

And I think this would be a very interesting extension of their business if they're not doing this type of thing already to be able to sell it, upsell it or cross sell to their farmer clients and bring those in as an extra piece of business.
So I think there would definitely be those two groups that we could market it to would be very interesting.
So I think there's a good opportunity and also there's a timing one as well because September is when everybody's back at their desks after having like two months of twiddling their thumbs.
In the summer, we do see this first week in particular where there's a massive interest spike.
So the sooner you guys get to market, the better, really.

I think it would be ambitious to say that we could get the deal done before Christmas, but certainly this final sort of sprint towards the end of the year, we do tend to see deals speed up in November and December to get them done before Christmas.
But I think realistically it is a six month process, however way you look at it.
So most likely it will be a deal that we could get done before sort of March, April time next year.
But, but it's, it's a, it is a, it's a, it's a great time because there's been a lot of activity in M and A.
Again, there's been a little bit of a slowdown.
Sorry, my dog's.
There's been a little bit of a slowdown in previous years, but since Trump won.
So that was one thing that was kind of a decider for good or bad, but it meant that there was a lot of people holding off, that they didn't know which way it was going to go.
So we've definitely seen this year pick up as well.
So I think there's a big opportunity and then in terms of what we do, because we actually work mostly in the U.S. as well, probably 90, 95% of our business, business is us.
I think it's quite likely that there's going to be a US buyer for the business and it would help, like you said before, Robin, if they wanted to Extend into Canada and they weren't there before.
I think it's a good opportunity just to round out the whole of North America if they're not doing it already.
So I think there is plenty of opportunity for buyers for this sort of business.
Mm.
Yeah.
I mean, you know, we're not as big, we don't spend as much per capita on medicines in Canada as we do in the US but we're still higher than Europe, you know, so.
So for a US Company wanting to look into Canada, it's still favorable.
It's not as favorable because they have a lot more latitude with branded advertising.
We have to be much more strategic in our messaging because we're not allowed to advertise brands directly to the public.
But we know how to do that, we know how to do that successfully.
So yeah, so it could appeal to them.
I think the, the market has changed in the US quite a bit.
